en: Having completed all the ritual activities within the mandala with colored powders,
the wise one should perform the dismissal by means of the power of meditative cultivation.
Having entered the mandala hall, he should gaze upon the mandala.
Since all phenomena arise dependently by their very nature,
from where has the maṇḍala, the deities of the maṇḍala, and likewise the lord of the maṇḍala come? And where will they go now?
Having observed that all this great [universe], including the Buddhas of the three times, is devoid of intrinsic nature,
free from both meditator and object of meditation, and by its very nature equal to space— resembling a dream, a city of Gandharvas, a mirage, or water in a mirage; [9.4]
Resembling an illusion or a mirage, like the pith of a plantain tree or a bubble of foam—
this entire world, though appearing as a shimmering variety, is devoid of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Resembling light and space, its characteristic is non-abiding.
Immediately thereafter, the red [deity], having drawn [the object] in by means of the rays of knowledge from the deities of the wheel,
establishes it in the expanse of the sky, in whatever manner [is appropriate].
Starting from the eastern gate, one should then pierce the four gates and even the corners with the wrathful vajras of one’s own hands,
while reciting the mantra *kṛto va* and finally the syllable *mūḥ*.
One should discard the portion of dust and then cause the milk to flow. Having gathered it in a clockwise direction, the venerable one,
who is esteemed by the Noble Ones, holding the bell and vajra, and bearing the pride of the deity, should act.
Having performed the sweeping with cow dung together with a suitable Yoginī,
one should offer the libation there during the evening at the gathering of the Gaṇas.
One should prepare colored powders in a victory-granting jar adorned with cloth.
Everything, beginning with the offering of bali and preceded by the rites of *argha* and so forth,
accompanied by the sounds of cymbals, drums, and excellent musical instruments, as well as the chanting of the *caryā*,
the vows, and other liturgical songs.
There, at the gatherings of yoginīs, which are gladdened by the joy of passion,
the master or the disciple of yoga, mounted upon a vehicle such as an elephant and so forth, [is present]. (9.13) [Is "yogya" intended for "anne"?]

Everywhere they were provided with betel-leaf, their bodies beautifully anointed with sandalwood paste. They were accompanied by foot-soldiers who bore various fruits and were adorned with the terrifying sounds of moving *ghargharikā* bells. [9.14–9.15]
Having gone to a lake of *nāgas* or to a place where deep water stands,
or else, if such is not available, the wise person should descend into a river that flows toward the ocean;
there, having sat upon a comfortable seat or even directly on the auspicious ground, [he should practice].
Having prepared a maṇḍala there with cow dung smeared over and perfumes and so forth,
one should then summon the nāgas by means of the masses of light rays from the seed-syllable in the heart;
one should then place them upon the eastern petal of an eight-petaled lotus in that maṇḍala.
Vāsuki on the southern lotus petal, Karkoṭaka on the western petal,
Takṣaka in the north, and Mahāpadma in the northeast;
Śaṅkhapāla in the southeast and Kulika in the southwest.

In the wind [direction], having brought the one named Huluṇḍa and likewise Vajrin in the filaments, the best of mantra-practitioners should perform the offering of *argha* and so forth, and worship them. Oṃ śrīvajrasattvāya hūṃ svāhā.
Oṃ vāsuki hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ padma hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ kārkoṭaka hūṃ svāhā |
Oṃ takṣaka hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ mahāpadma hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ śaṅkhapāla hūṃ svāhā |
Oṃ kuliśapāla hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ huluṇḍa hūṃ svāhā | [Offer] flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings accompanied by fragrance.
Having given [the gift], he should indeed speak these words for the sake of receiving the pollen:
"In this world-system, a mandala has been drawn by me, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, for the sake of my disciples; may you all rejoice in it. [9.21-9.22]
Having performed this, may they receive the dust for the sake of the gift, the Lord, and the welfare [of beings];
and furthermore, by your grace, may the teaching endure for a long time.
Immediately thereafter, they were indeed filled with joy and born of gladness.
Preceded by the sounds of musical instruments, songs, and dances from their own respective divine courtyards, they—
adorned with joined palms raised to their heads in respectful salutation—
swiftly receive the dust, acting as the upholders of the Buddha’s command.
Thinking, "It has been released," the wise one descended into the water and caused the mass of dust to flow away by pouring milk into it.
Then the nāgas, taking up the dust, went quickly to their own abode.
And with joy and in detail, they spoke again within their respective families:
"Jambudvīpa is auspicious and supreme if it contains this collection of mantras;
where this half [of the teaching] exists, there the sentient beings will partake in awakening—of this there is no doubt. [9.28]
Then, having gratified him with gifts of betel nut and the like, or with passion,
the wise one returns, contemplating the nature of reality. [9.29]
Thus concludes the procedure for the dismissal of the dust.
